claim: MYCBP was consistently identified as an interacting partner of the Astrin-SKAP complex in human tissue culture cells.
source: In addition to the previously defined subunits Astrin, SKAP, and LC8, we consistently identified MYCBP as an interacting partner (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data from immunoprecipitations shown in Figure 1A

claim: MYCBP localizes to kinetochores only after chromosome alignment.
source: Supporting its interaction as a component of the Astrin-SKAP complex, MYCBP localizes to kinetochores only after chromosome alignment (Figure 1B)
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1B

claim: MYCBP kinetochore localization depends on Astrin and SKAP.
source: MYCBP localizes to kinetochores only after chromosome alignment (Figure 1B) and in an Astrin and SKAP-dependent manner (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by depletion experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: The Astrin-SKAP complex is a 4-subunit complex containing Astrin, SKAP, LC8, and MYCBP.
source: We were able to isolate a complex containing full length versions of each protein that co-purified over Ni-NTA resin and size exclusion chromatography (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by biochemical purification data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B

claim: Astrin residues 694-1193 are not required for the associations within the Astrin-SKAP complex.
source: Truncating the C-terminal half of Astrin by removing residues 694–1193 (Astrin 1–693) did not alter the associations within the Astrin-SKAP complex and resulted in increased expression of a well-behaved complex (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by biochemical purification data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B

claim: Astrin residues 465-693 are sufficient to interact with SKAP, LC8, and MYCBP.
source: Finally, we found that a region containing the central coiled-coil region of Astrin (residues 465–693) migrated appropriately by gel filtration and was sufficient to interact with SKAP, LC8, and MYCBP (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by biochemical purification and gel filtration data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B

claim: Eliminating the TQT motif in Astrin (residues 465-482) disrupts the interaction between Astrin and LC8 but does not alter SKAP or MYCBP binding.
source: Within this 465–693 region of Astrin, eliminating a small predicted loop (residues 465–482) containing a 'TQT' motif implicated in LC8 binding (Lo et al., 2001) disrupted the interaction between Astrin and LC8, but did not alter SKAP or MYCBP binding (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by biochemical purification data shown in Figure 1C and citation to prior work on LC8 binding motifs

claim: The Astrin-SKAP complex has a 2:2:2:2 stoichiometry.
source: Fitting of the AUC data indicated a single major species was present (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E). The molecular weight of this species fit to a complex with 2:2:2:2 stoichiometry (see Materials and methods).
evidence: Supported by analytical ultracentrifugation data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E

claim: The Astrin 1-693 complex binds to microtubules with an apparent affinity of 3.2 µM.
source: The complex containing the N-terminal Astrin region (1-693) bound to microtubules with an apparent affinity of 3.2 µM (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: Supported by microtubule co-sedimentation assay data shown in Figure 2A,B

claim: The SKAP 5xD charge swap mutant eliminates the binding of the Astrin-SKAP complex to microtubules in vitro.
source: In contrast, we found that a charge swap mutant in SKAP ('5xD'), which substantially reduced Astrin-SKAP complex spindle microtubule localization in cells (Kern et al., 2016), also eliminates the binding of the Astrin-SKAP complex to microtubules in vitro (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by microtubule binding assay data shown in Figure 2A and citation to prior work

claim: The Astrin-SKAP complex decorates and bundles microtubules.
source: Furthermore, the Astrin-SKAP complex decorated and bundled microtubules based on negative stain transmission electron microscopy (Figure 2C)
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2C

claim: The Astrin N-terminus (aa 1-693) localizes to microtubules in cells.
source: In cells, the Astrin N-terminus (aa 1–693) localized to microtubules (Figure 3B)
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3B

claim: The Astrin N-terminus (aa 1-693) localizes only weakly to kinetochores.
source: In cells, the Astrin N-terminus (aa 1–693) localized to microtubules (Figure 3B), consistent with its ability to interact with the SKAP microtubule binding subunit (Figure 1C). However, Astrin 1–693 localized only weakly to kinetochores.
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3B

claim: The Astrin C-terminus (aa 694-1193) localizes to kinetochores but not microtubules.
source: In contrast, the Astrin C-terminus (aa 694–1193), which lacks the SKAP binding site, localized to kinetochores, but not microtubules (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3B

claim: The Astrin C-terminus only localizes to bi-oriented kinetochores.
source: Notably, similar to full length Astrin, the Astrin C-terminus only localized to bi-oriented kinetochores (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Cells in which the Astrin C-terminus replaced endogenous Astrin displayed dramatically reduced localization of SKAP to kinetochores.
source: As predicted based on the inability of the Astrin C-terminus to bind SKAP, cells in which the Astrin C-terminus replaced endogenous Astrin displayed dramatically reduced localization of SKAP to kinetochores (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3C

claim: Depletion of Astrin using an inducible knockout system results in increased mitotic cells with misaligned chromosomes and multipolar spindles.
source: Depletion of Astrin using the inducible knockout system resulted in a pronounced increase in mitotic cells with misaligned chromosomes and multipolar spindles (Figure 3D), hallmarks of defective kinetochore function.
evidence: Supported by quantification of mitotic defects shown in Figure 3D

claim: Expression of full length Astrin rescues chromosome segregation defects caused by Astrin depletion.
source: These defects were rescued by expression of full length Astrin, but not by expression of the Astrin 694–1193 truncation (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 3D

claim: Expression of Astrin 694-1193 does not rescue chromosome segregation defects caused by Astrin depletion.
source: These defects were rescued by expression of full length Astrin, but not by expression of the Astrin 694–1193 truncation (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 3D

claim: Astrin 465-1193 rescues major chromosome segregation defects caused by Astrin depletion.
source: However, a shorter Astrin truncation (465–1193), which preserves the SKAP interaction, rescued these major chromosome segregation defects (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 3D

claim: The Astrin-SKAP complex interacts with the Ndc80 complex at kinetochores in cells.
source: In contrast, when we used our cross-linking protocol, we additionally isolated the kinetochore-localized Ndc80 complex (Figure 4C), the core component of the kinetochore-microtubule interface (Cheeseman et al., 2006; DeLuca et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by cross-linking immunoprecipitation mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4C and citations to prior work on Ndc80

claim: Peptides for the Ndc80/Hec1 and Nuf2 subunits were identified across multiple replicates of cross-linking immunoprecipitation experiments.
source: Peptides for the Ndc80/Hec1 and Nuf2 subunits in particular were identified across multiple replicates of this experiment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C

claim: The Astrin-SKAP complex displays enhanced binding to microtubules in the presence of 1 µM Ndc80 Bonsai complex.
source: In contrast, we found that the Astrin-SKAP complex displayed enhanced binding to microtubules in the presence of 1 µM Ndc80 Bonsai complex (Figure 5A), an internally truncated and shortened complex (Ciferri et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by microtubule binding assay data shown in Figure 5A and citation to prior work on Ndc80 Bonsai

claim: The apparent KD of the Astrin-SKAP complex for microtubules is ~3.2 µM alone versus 1.4 µM in the presence of the Ndc80 Bonsai complex.
source: We observed an apparent KD of ~3.2 µM for the Astrin-SKAP complex alone vs. 1.4 µM in the presence of the Ndc80 Bonsai complex.
evidence: Supported by quantification of microtubule binding assays

claim: The SKAP 5xD mutant complex fails to bind to microtubules even in the presence of the Ndc80 complex.
source: This altered binding requires a direct interaction between SKAP and the microtubule, as the SKAP 5xD mutant complex failed to bind to microtubules even in the presence of the Ndc80 complex (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by microtubule binding assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A

claim: The Astrin-SKAP complex shows enhanced apparent binding in the presence of the Ndc80 Broccoli complex.
source: We also observed enhanced apparent binding of the Astrin-SKAP complex in the presence of the Ndc80 Broccoli complex (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: Supported by microtubule binding assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B

claim: The Ndc80 CH domain (aa 1-201) increases the apparent microtubule binding of the Astrin-SKAP complex.
source: Additionally, we tested binding of the Astrin-SKAP complex to microtubules in the presence of an Ndc80 calponin homology domain (CH Domain) (aa 1–201) (Hiruma et al., 2015). Even though this construct binds microtubules more poorly than the complete Ndc80 complex, it was also able to increase the apparent microtubule binding of the Astrin-SKAP complex (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: Supported by microtubule binding assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and citation to prior work

claim: The Ndc80 1-201 region contains the interaction site for the Astrin-SKAP complex.
source: Even though this construct binds microtubules more poorly than the complete Ndc80 complex, it was also able to increase the apparent microtubule binding of the Astrin-SKAP complex (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that the Ndc80 1–201 region contains the interaction site.
evidence: Inferred from the ability of the Ndc80 CH domain to enhance Astrin-SKAP microtubule binding

claim: The Astrin-SKAP complex is able to bind robustly to microtubules even at saturating concentrations of Ndc80 complex.
source: Interestingly, even at the highest saturating concentrations of Ndc80 complex, the Astrin-SKAP complex was still able to bind robustly to the microtubule-Ndc80 complex, indicating that these complexes are able to bind to microtubules simultaneously.
evidence: Supported by microtubule binding assays with varying Ndc80 concentrations shown in Figure 5B

claim: The Ndc80 and Astrin-SKAP complexes are able to bind to microtubules simultaneously.
source: Interestingly, even at the highest saturating concentrations of Ndc80 complex, the Astrin-SKAP complex was still able to bind robustly to the microtubule-Ndc80 complex, indicating that these complexes are able to bind to microtubules simultaneously.
evidence: Supported by microtubule binding assays with varying Ndc80 concentrations shown in Figure 5B

claim: The C. elegans NDC-80 complex displays competitive interactions with the Astrin-SKAP complex at high NDC-80 concentrations.
source: However, in contrast to the cooperative interactions with the human Ndc80 complex, we found that the C. elegans NDC-80 complex displayed competitive interactions with the Astrin-SKAP complex at high NDC-80 concentrations (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by microtubule binding assay data shown in Figure 5B

claim: The synergistic interaction between the Astrin-SKAP and Ndc80 complexes requires sequences or features specific to the human Ndc80 complex.
source: Therefore, the synergistic interaction we observed requires sequences or features specific to the human Ndc80 complex.
evidence: Inferred from the competitive interaction observed with C. elegans NDC-80 complex versus cooperative interaction with human Ndc80 complex

claim: The Astrin N-terminal domain (1-464) is required for robust interactions with the Ndc80 complex.
source: We also found that the N-terminus of Astrin is required to achieve robust interactions with the Ndc80 complex. Removing the Astrin N-terminal domain (1-464) significantly compromised its interaction with the Ndc80 complex
evidence: Supported by microtubule binding assays comparing Astrin 1-693 and Astrin 465-693 complexes shown in Figure 5C,D

claim: The Astrin 465-693 complex displays only a modest enhancement of its microtubule binding activity in the presence of 1 µM Ndc80 complex (KD ~2.2 µM vs. 1.7 µM).
source: First, the Astrin 465–693 complex displayed only a modest enhancement of its microtubule binding activity in the presence of 1 µM Ndc80 complex (KD ~2.2 µM vs. 1.7 µM; Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by microtubule binding assay data shown in Figure 5C

claim: The Astrin 465-693 complex is competed off of microtubules at increasing Ndc80 complex concentrations.
source: Second, the Astrin 465–693 complex was competed off of microtubules at increasing Ndc80 complex concentrations (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by microtubule binding assay data shown in Figure 5D

claim: The Astrin-SKAP complex displays a unique localization timing to bi-oriented kinetochores.
source: In contrast to other established components of the kinetochore-microtubule interface, the Astrin-SKAP complex displays a unique localization timing to bi-oriented kinetochores (Figure 3A, Figure 3—video 1, and Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3A, Figure 3—video 1, and Figure 6A

claim: The Astrin-SKAP complex localizes to correctly attached kinetochores at a time of high kinetochore tension, just prior to chromosome separation and segregation at anaphase onset.
source: This late mitotic localization brings the Astrin-SKAP complex to correctly attached kinetochores at a time of high kinetochore tension, just prior to chromosome separation and segregation at anaphase onset.
evidence: Inferred from the observed localization timing of the Astrin-SKAP complex

claim: The Astrin-SKAP complex plays a critical role in chromosome segregation in human cells based on RNAi-based depletions and CRISPR/Cas9-based inducible knockouts.
source: The Astrin-SKAP complex plays a critical role in chromosome segregation in human cells based on both RNAi-based depletions (Dunsch et al., 2011; Kern et al., 2016; Manning et al., 2010) and CRISPR/Cas9-based inducible knockouts ([McKinley and Cheeseman, 2017]; this study).
evidence: Supported by depletion and knockout experiments cited and shown in this study

claim: The SKAP microtubule-binding activity is required for proper chromosome segregation.
source: In particular, we and others have recently shown that the SKAP microtubule-binding activity is required for proper chromosome segregation (Friese et al., 2016; Kern et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: The Astrin-SKAP complex is conserved throughout vertebrates.
source: Intriguingly, although the Astrin-SKAP complex is conserved throughout vertebrates, SKAP and Astrin knockouts in mice and rats have shown that this complex is dispensable for viability in rodents (Grey et al., 2016; Xue et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work on Astrin-SKAP conservation and knockout studies

claim: SKAP and Astrin knockouts in mice and rats show that the Astrin-SKAP complex is dispensable for viability in rodents.
source: Intriguingly, although the Astrin-SKAP complex is conserved throughout vertebrates, SKAP and Astrin knockouts in mice and rats have shown that this complex is dispensable for viability in rodents (Grey et al., 2016; Xue et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: The SKAP binding site on Astrin is located within residues 482-693.
source: Here, we further refine the SKAP binding site on Astrin using complex reconstitution and cell biological approaches to residues 482–693.
evidence: Supported by biochemical reconstitution data shown in Figure 1C

claim: The Astrin C-terminal domain (amino acids 694-1193) is sufficient for kinetochore localization.
source: We additionally identify a C-terminal Astrin domain (amino acids 694–1193) that is sufficient for kinetochore localization.
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3B

claim: The Astrin-SKAP complex is a multimeric microtubule binder due to the presence of two copies of the SKAP microtubule binding subunit per complex.
source: First, the Astrin-SKAP complex is a multimeric microtubule binder due to the presence of two copies of the SKAP microtubule binding subunit per complex as defined by our analysis of Astrin-SKAP complex stoichiometry.
evidence: Inferred from the 2:2:2:2 stoichiometry determined by AUC

claim: The human Ndc80 complex has a well-defined binding site and angle on microtubules.
source: The human Ndc80 complex has a well-defined binding site and angle on microtubules and is able to bind at every tubulin monomer within the microtubule lattice using the 'toe' region of its CH domain.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior structural work

claim: The Ndc80 complex interacts with the negatively-charged E-hook of tubulin using its positively charged N-terminal tail.
source: In addition, the Ndc80 complex interacts with the negatively-charged E-hook of tubulin using its positively charged N-terminal tail (Alushin et al., 2012, 2010) (Wilson-Kubalek et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior structural work

claim: A small piece of SKAP containing its microtubule binding domain reciprocally competes with the Ndc80 complex for microtubule binding.
source: Indeed, Friese et al. (2016) recently noted that a small piece of SKAP, containing its microtubule binding domain, reciprocally competes with the Ndc80 complex for microtubule binding.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work

claim: SKAP's microtubule binding domain is positively charged and predicted to be unstructured.
source: Similar to Ndc80's N-terminal tail, SKAP's microtubule binding domain is positively charged and predicted to be unstructured
evidence: Based on sequence analysis and comparison to Ndc80

claim: Astrin's interaction with Ndc80 may position SKAP to access the conformation of the Ndc80-bound E-hook.
source: Astrin's interaction with Ndc80 may position SKAP to access the conformation of the Ndc80-bound E-hook (Alushin et al., 2012).
evidence: Speculative model based on structural considerations and citation to prior work

claim: In cells, SKAP may access microtubule regions beyond the reach of kinetochore-tethered Ndc80.
source: Furthermore, in cells, SKAP may access microtubule regions beyond the reach of kinetochore-tethered Ndc80 (Schmidt et al., 2010).
evidence: Speculative model based on citation to prior work

claim: The Astrin-SKAP complex has two binding sites at kinetochores: the kinetochore-bound microtubule and the Ndc80 complex.
source: Due to the unique localization timing of the Astrin-SKAP complex, its regulation is an intriguing problem. Our work defines two Astrin-SKAP binding sites at kinetochores - the kinetochore-bound microtubule and the Ndc80 complex.
evidence: Supported by biochemical and cell biological data throughout the manuscript

claim: The Astrin-SKAP complex is fully active for kinetochore binding only when Ndc80 is docked on kinetochore microtubules.
source: We propose a model in which Astrin-SKAP is fully active for kinetochore binding only when Ndc80 is docked on kinetochore microtubules.
evidence: Proposed model based on the observed interactions and localization dependencies

claim: The Astrin-SKAP complex acts in the opposite manner of the Mps1 checkpoint protein, which competes with microtubules for free Ndc80 complex.
source: In this case, the Astrin-SKAP complex would act in the opposite manner of the Mps1 checkpoint protein, which has been shown to compete with microtubules for free Ndc80 complex (Hiruma et al., 2015; Ji et al., 2015).
evidence: Proposed model based on comparison to prior work on Mps1

claim: The C-terminus of Astrin contains a kinetochore interaction domain.
source: In addition to the microtubule-dependent interactions, we find that the C-terminus of Astrin contains a kinetochore interaction domain and localizes to kinetochores with similar localization timing to the full-length complex, despite an inability to bind to microtubules (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by localization data shown in Figure 3

claim: Peptides from the CENP-L/N complex and the Dsn1 subunit of the Mis12 complex were sporadically obtained in cross-linking immunoprecipitations of Astrin.
source: We note that we sporadically obtained peptides from the CENP-L/N complex and the Dsn1 subunit of the Mis12 complex in our cross-linking immunoprecipitations of Astrin (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C

claim: Reciprocal immunoprecipitations of the CENP-L-N complex isolated the Astrin-SKAP complex.
source: Reciprocal immunoprecipitations of the CENP-L-N complex also isolated the Astrin-SKAP complex (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), supporting a potential association.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D

claim: Astrin's long coiled-coil domains would allow it to span large distances from inner kinetochore locations to the microtubule interface.
source: Theoretically, Astrin's long coiled-coil domains would allow it to span large distances from these inner kinetochore locations to the microtubule interface.
evidence: Speculative model based on structural considerations

claim: Astrin's C-terminus could bind to a secondary location on the Ndc80 complex.
source: Alternatively, Astrin's C-terminus could bind to a secondary location on the Ndc80 complex.
evidence: Speculative alternative model

claim: The Astrin-SKAP complex is the final component of the outer kinetochore that is recruited prior to anaphase onset.
source: Thus, the Astrin-SKAP complex is the final component of the outer kinetochore that is recruited prior to anaphase onset.
evidence: Inferred from the unique localization timing observed

claim: The Astrin-SKAP complex may act to stabilize proper kinetochore-microtubule attachments to ensure correct chromosome segregation during metaphase and anaphase.
source: Thus, the Astrin-SKAP complex may act to stabilize proper kinetochore-microtubule attachments to ensure correct chromosome segregation during metaphase and anaphase.
evidence: Proposed model based on localization timing and functional data

claim: The Astrin-SKAP complex acts together with the Ndc80 complex to stabilize correctly formed kinetochore-microtubule interactions.
source: We propose a model in which the Astrin-SKAP complex acts together with the Ndc80 complex to stabilize correctly formed kinetochore-microtubule interactions.
evidence: Proposed model based on biochemical and cell biological data

claim: Astrin displays dynamic localization to kinetochores during mitosis and only localizes to aligned and bi-oriented kinetochores.
source: In an important contrast to other components of the kinetochore-microtubule interface, the Astrin-SKAP complex associates dynamically with kinetochores during mitosis and only localizes to aligned and bi-oriented kinetochores (Friese et al., 2016; Mack and Compton, 2001; Manning et al., 2010; Schmidt et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: The Ndc80 complex is the core microtubule-binding unit of the kinetochore and is widely conserved across eukaryotes.
source: The Ndc80 complex is the core microtubule binding unit of the kinetochore and is widely conserved across eukaryotes.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge

claim: The Ndc80 complex associates with microtubules using a precise binding site and angled orientation.
source: The Ndc80 complex associates with microtubules using a precise binding site and angled orientation (Alushin et al., 2010; Wilson-Kubalek et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior structural work

claim: In budding yeast, the Dam1 complex provides a ring-like coupler to stably attach each kinetochore to a depolymerizing microtubule by conferring processivity to the Ndc80 complex.
source: In budding yeast, the Dam1 complex provides a ring-like coupler to stably attach each kinetochore to a depolymerizing microtubule by conferring processivity to the Ndc80 complex (Lampert et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work

claim: In metazoans, the Ska1 complex adds additional microtubule binding and confers its microtubule-tracking ability to the Ndc80 complex.
source: In metazoans, the Ska1 complex adds additional microtubule binding and confers its microtubule-tracking ability to the Ndc80 complex (Schmidt et al., 2012; Welburn et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: A complex of Astrin, SKAP, and the dynein light-chain LC8 localizes to both kinetochores and spindle microtubules.
source: We and others previously isolated a complex of Astrin, SKAP, and the dynein light-chain LC8 from human cells that localizes to both kinetochores and spindle microtubules (Dunsch et al., 2011; Schmidt et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: Astrin and SKAP play critical roles in chromosome segregation and the maintenance of spindle bipolarity based on depletion and knockout experiments in human cells.
source: Astrin and SKAP play critical roles in chromosome segregation and the maintenance of spindle bipolarity based on depletion and knockout experiments in human cells (Dunsch et al., 2011; Friese et al., 2016; Gruber et al., 2002; Kern et al., 2016; Mack and Compton, 2001; Manning et al., 2010; McKinley and Cheeseman, 2017; Schmidt et al., 2010; Thein et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: SKAP possesses a microtubule plus-end tracking activity through its interaction with EB family proteins.
source: First, SKAP possesses a microtubule plus-end tracking activity through its interaction with EB family proteins (Friese et al., 2016; Kern et al., 2016; Tamura et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: SKAP plus-end tracking is required for proper interactions of astral microtubules with the cell cortex and metaphase spindle positioning, but not for chromosome segregation.
source: SKAP plus-end tracking is required for proper interactions of astral microtubules with the cell cortex and metaphase spindle positioning, but not for chromosome segregation (Kern et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work

claim: SKAP binds directly to microtubules, and mutants that precisely disrupt microtubule binding result in dramatic defects in chromosome alignment and segregation.
source: Second, SKAP binds directly to microtubules, and mutants that precisely disrupt microtubule binding result in dramatic defects in chromosome alignment and segregation (Friese et al., 2016; Kern et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: MYCBP interacts with AKAP family proteins and ARFGEF1.
source: In reciprocal immunoprecipitations, MYCBP isolated the Astrin-SKAP complex, as well as some of its previously defined interactors, including the AKAP family proteins and ARFGEF1 (Furusawa et al., 2001; Furusawa et al., 2002; Ishizaki et al., 2006; Taira et al., 1998) (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1A and citations to prior work
